| --- | --- | --- |
| .png | Image | IMAGE |
| .jpg / .jpeg | Image | IMAGE |
| .webp | Image | IMAGE |
| .html / .htm | Document | DOCUMENT |

HTML files are uploaded as document screens — useful for importing static snapshots of existing web pages or prototypes.

### Options

Section titled “Options”

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| title | string | — | Display title for the screen in Stitch |
| createScreenInstances | boolean | true | Whether to add the screen to the canvas |

### Upload HTML prototypes

Section titled “Upload HTML prototypes”

Upload a self-contained HTML file to import an existing design:

```
const result = await project.upload("./prototype.html", {
  title: "Landing Page Prototype",
});
```

The SDK detects `.html` and `.htm` extensions automatically and sets the screen type to `DOCUMENT`.

### Handle results

Section titled “Handle results”

`upload()` never throws. It returns a discriminated result object:

```
const result = await project.upload("./mockup.png");

if (result.success) {
  console.log(`Created ${result.screens.length} screens`);
} else {
  console.error(`${result.error.code}: ${result.error.message}`);
}
```

#### Error codes

Section titled “Error codes”

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| FILE_NOT_FOUND | File doesn’t exist at the given path |
| UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT | Extension isn’t .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .webp, .html, or .htm |
| AUTH_FAILED | Invalid or missing API key |
| UPLOAD_FAILED | Server rejected the upload |
| UNKNOWN_ERROR | Unexpected failure |

### Bulk upload

Section titled “Bulk upload”

Upload multiple files in a loop:

```
import fs from "fs/promises";
import path from "path";

const project = stitch.project("your-project-id");
const files = await fs.readdir("./designs");

for (const file of files) {
  if (/\.(png|jpe?g|webp|html?)$/i.test(file)) {
    const result = await project.upload(
      path.join("./designs", file),
      { title: path.parse(file).name },
    );
    if (result.success) {
      console.log(`Uploaded ${file} → ${result.screens[0].id}`);
    }
  }
}
```
## Reference

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/sdk/reference/

Complete API reference for the Stitch TypeScript SDK.

### Installation

Section titled “Installation”

```
npm install @google/stitch-sdk
```

### Exports

Section titled “Exports”

All exports are available from `@google/stitch-sdk`:

```
import {
  stitch,           // Default singleton instance
  Stitch,           // Domain class: project management
  Project,          // Domain class: screen management within a project
  Screen,           // Domain class: screen operations
  StitchToolClient, // Low-level MCP client
  StitchProxy,      // Local proxy server
  StitchError,      // Error class
  StitchErrorCode,  // Error code enum
} from "@google/stitch-sdk";
```

AI SDK adapter (separate subpath):

```
import { stitchTools } from "@google/stitch-sdk/ai";
```

### stitch (Singleton)

Section titled “stitch (Singleton)”

The default entry point. A lazily-initialized `Proxy` that combines `Stitch` domain methods and `StitchToolClient` infrastructure methods.

Reads `STITCH_API_KEY` and `STITCH_HOST` from environment variables on first access.

```
import { stitch } from "@google/stitch-sdk";
```

#### Domain methods

Section titled “Domain methods”

| Method | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| createProject(title) | Promise<Project> | Creates a new project. |
| projects() | Promise<Project[]> | Lists all projects accessible to the authenticated user. |
| project(id) | Project | Creates a Project handle from an existing project ID or resource name. No API call. |

#### Infrastructure methods

Section titled “Infrastructure methods”

| Method | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| listTools() | Promise<{ tools: ToolDefinition[] }> | Lists all available MCP tools. |
| callTool<T>(name, params) | Promise<T> | Calls a raw MCP tool by name. |
| close() | Promise<void> | Closes the underlying MCP client connection. |

### Stitch

Section titled “Stitch”

Main entry point class. Manages projects.

```
import { Stitch, StitchToolClient } from "@google/stitch-sdk";

const client = new StitchToolClient({ apiKey: "..." });
const s = new Stitch(client);
```

#### Constructor

Section titled “Constructor”

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| client | StitchToolClient | An initialized tool client instance. |

#### Methods

Section titled “Methods”

| Method | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| createProject(title) | Promise<Project> | Creates a new project. Maps to MCP tool create_project. |
| projects() | Promise<Project[]> | Lists all projects. Maps to MCP tool list_projects. |
| project(id) | Project | Creates a Project handle without an API call. Accepts a project ID or full resource name (projects/{id}). |

### Project

Section titled “Project”

A Stitch project containing screens.

#### Properties

Section titled “Properties”

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| projectId | string | The project ID (without projects/ prefix). |
| id | string | Alias for projectId. |
| data | any | Raw API response data, if constructed from server response. undefined if constructed from an ID string. |

#### Methods

Section titled “Methods”

| Method | Parameters | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| generate(prompt, deviceType?, modelId?) | prompt: string, deviceType?: DeviceType, modelId?: ModelId | Promise<Screen> | Generates a new screen from a text prompt. Maps to generate_screen_from_text. |
| screens() | - | Promise<Screen[]> | Lists all screens in the project. Maps to list_screens. |
| getScreen(screenId) | screenId: string | Promise<Screen> | Retrieves a specific screen by ID. Maps to get_screen. |
| upload(filePath, opts?) | filePath: string, opts?: { title?: string, createScreenInstances?: boolean } | Promise<UploadResult> | Uploads a file (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .webp, .html, .htm) and creates a screen. Posts directly to REST API. Never throws — returns a discriminated result. |
| createDesignSystem(ds) | ds: { displayName: string } | Promise<DesignSystem> | Creates a design system for this project. |
| listDesignSystems() | - | Promise<DesignSystem[]> | Lists all design systems in the project. |
| designSystem(id) | id: string | DesignSystem | Creates a DesignSystem handle from an asset ID. No API call. |

### DesignSystem

Section titled “DesignSystem”

A design system asset that defines visual tokens for a project.

#### Properties

Section titled “Properties”

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| id | string | The asset ID. |
| data | any | Raw API response data. undefined if constructed from an ID string. |

#### Methods

Section titled “Methods”

| Method | Parameters | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| update(ds) | ds: { displayName?: string } | Promise<DesignSystem> | Updates the design system’s metadata. |
| apply(selectedScreenInstances) | { id: string, sourceScreen: string }[] | Promise<Screen[]> | Applies this design system to the given screens. Only pass id and sourceScreen — extra fields cause errors. |

### Screen

Section titled “Screen”

A generated UI screen. Provides access to HTML code and screenshot images.

#### Properties

Section titled “Properties”

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| projectId | string | Parent project ID. |
| screenId | string | The screen ID. |
| id | string | Alias for screenId. |
| data | any | Raw API response data. |

#### Methods

Section titled “Methods”

| Method | Parameters | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| edit(prompt, deviceType?, modelId?) | prompt: string, deviceType?: DeviceType, modelId?: ModelId | Promise<Screen> | Edits this screen with a text prompt. Returns a new Screen; original is unchanged. Maps to edit_screens. |
| variants(prompt, variantOptions, deviceType?, modelId?) | prompt: string, variantOptions: VariantOptions, deviceType?: DeviceType, modelId?: ModelId | Promise<Screen[]> | Generates design variants. Maps to generate_variants. |
| getHtml() | - | Promise<string> | Returns the HTML download URL for this screen. Uses cached URL if available. |
| getImage() | - | Promise<string> | Returns the screenshot download URL. Uses cached URL if available. |

### StitchToolClient

Section titled “StitchToolClient”

Low-level MCP client that connects to the Stitch server over HTTP.

```
import { StitchToolClient } from "@google/stitch-sdk";
```

#### Constructor

Section titled “Constructor”

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| config | StitchConfigInput | Connection configuration. |

#### StitchConfigInput

Section titled “StitchConfigInput”

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| apiKey | string | One of apiKey or accessToken | API key for authentication. |
| accessToken | string | One of apiKey or accessToken | OAuth access token. |
| projectId | string | Required with accessToken | Google Cloud project ID (for OAuth). |
| baseUrl | string | No | Override the server URL. Defaults to https://stitch.googleapis.com/mcp. |

#### Methods

Section titled “Methods”

| Method | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| connect() | Promise<void> | Explicitly connects to the MCP server. Called automatically on first tool call. |
| callTool<T>(name, params) | Promise<T> | Calls a named MCP tool with the given parameters. |
| listTools() | Promise<{ tools: ToolDefinition[] }> | Lists all available tools from the server. |
| close() | Promise<void> | Closes the connection. |

### stitchTools(options?)

Section titled “stitchTools(options?)”

AI SDK adapter. Returns Stitch tools in Vercel AI SDK format.

Import from the `/ai` subpath:

```
import { stitchTools } from "@google/stitch-sdk/ai";
```

#### Parameters

Section titled “Parameters”

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| options.apiKey | string | Override STITCH_API_KEY env var. |
| options.include | string[] | Only include specific tool names. |

#### Returns

Section titled “Returns”

`Record<string, Tool>` - Drop directly into `generateText({ tools: stitchTools() })`.

### StitchError

Section titled “StitchError”

Error class thrown by all SDK methods.

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| message | string | Human-readable error message. |
| code | StitchErrorCode | Structured error code. |

#### Static methods

Section titled “Static methods”

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| StitchError.fromUnknown(error) | Wraps any thrown value into a StitchError. |

### Enums

Section titled “Enums”

#### DeviceType

Section titled “DeviceType”

`"DEVICE_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED"` | `"MOBILE"` | `"DESKTOP"` | `"TABLET"` | `"AGNOSTIC"`

#### ModelId

Section titled “ModelId”

`"MODEL_ID_UNSPECIFIED"` | `"GEMINI_3_PRO"` | `"GEMINI_3_FLASH"`

#### CreativeRange

Section titled “CreativeRange”

`"CREATIVE_RANGE_UNSPECIFIED"` | `"REFINE"` | `"EXPLORE"` | `"REIMAGINE"`

#### VariantAspect

Section titled “VariantAspect”

`"VARIANT_ASPECT_UNSPECIFIED"` | `"LAYOUT"` | `"COLOR_SCHEME"` | `"IMAGES"` | `"TEXT_FONT"` | `"TEXT_CONTENT"`

### Environment Variables

Section titled “Environment Variables”

| Variable | Description |
| --- | --- |
| STITCH_API_KEY | API key for authentication. Used by the stitch singleton and stitchTools(). |
| STITCH_HOST | Override the MCP server URL. Defaults to https://stitch.googleapis.com/mcp. |
| STITCH_ACCESS_TOKEN | OAuth access token (alternative to API key). |
| GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT | Google Cloud project ID (required with OAuth). |
## Architecture

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/sdk/architecture/

How the Stitch SDK is built and why it works the way it does.

The Stitch SDK isn’t a hand-written REST client. It’s a generated domain layer built on top of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), designed to give you a fluent TypeScript API while keeping a single source of truth for every tool Stitch offers.

### Why MCP, not REST?

Section titled “Why MCP, not REST?”

Stitch already runs an MCP server that AI agents connect to directly. Instead of maintaining a separate REST API surface, the SDK connects to the same MCP server over HTTP. This means:

- **One API surface.** The tools available to the SDK are the exact same tools your AI agent uses. No drift.
- **Instant updates.** When new tools ship on the MCP server, the SDK generator picks them up automatically.
- **Agent compatibility.** The same `callTool` semantics work whether you’re in an SDK script or an AI agent.

### The three layers

Section titled “The three layers”

The SDK has a clear three-layer architecture:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│     stitch (singleton proxy)     │  ← What you import
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Stitch / Project / Screen       │  ← Generated domain classes
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│       StitchToolClient           │  ← MCP-over-HTTP transport
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Layer 1: StitchToolClient (transport)

Section titled “Layer 1: StitchToolClient (transport)”

The foundation. Connects to the Stitch MCP server over HTTP, handles authentication (API key or OAuth), and exposes raw `callTool(name, params)` for any MCP tool. You can use this layer directly if you need full control.

#### Layer 2: Generated domain classes (domain)

Section titled “Layer 2: Generated domain classes (domain)”

`Stitch`, `Project`, and `Screen` are **auto-generated** from two source files:

1. **`tools-manifest.json`** - A snapshot of every MCP tool’s name, description, and input schema.
2. **`domain-map.json`** - A hand-authored mapping that assigns tools to domain classes and methods.

A generation script reads both files and produces TypeScript classes in `generated/src/`. Each method is a thin wrapper around `callTool` that handles parameter mapping and response parsing.

The generation is **content-hash locked** - regenerating only produces changes when the manifest or domain map actually changes. This prevents churn.

#### Layer 3: stitch singleton (convenience)

Section titled “Layer 3: stitch singleton (convenience)”

A `Proxy` object that lazily initializes a `StitchToolClient` from environment variables and delegates method calls to either the `Stitch` domain class or the `StitchToolClient`, depending on the method name.

When you write `stitch.projects()`, the proxy routes to `Stitch.projects()`. When you write `stitch.callTool(...)`, it routes to `StitchToolClient.callTool()`.

### Identity map pattern

Section titled “Identity map pattern”

`stitch.project(id)` and `new Project(client, id)` create a **handle** without making an API call. They parse the ID (stripping any `projects/` prefix) and return a `Project` object that you can immediately call `.generate()`, `.screens()`, or `.getScreen()` on.

This is useful when you already know a project ID from a previous operation - you don’t need to re-fetch it.

### The AI SDK adapter

Section titled “The AI SDK adapter”

`stitchTools()` (from `@google/stitch-sdk/ai`) bridges the SDK into the Vercel AI SDK ecosystem. It reads the same `tools-manifest.json` and produces a `Record<string, Tool>` compatible with `generateText()` and `streamText()`.

The adapter has **zero runtime dependency** on the `ai` package. It reconstructs the tool schema format using `Symbol.for("vercel.ai.schema")` - matching the AI SDK’s internal protocol without importing any of its code. This keeps the SDK lightweight for consumers who use only the domain API.

### Error handling

Section titled “Error handling”

All domain methods catch errors internally and re-throw them as `StitchError` instances with structured error codes. This gives you a single error type to catch:

```
import { StitchError } from "@google/stitch-sdk";

try {
  await screen.edit("...");
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof StitchError) {
    console.error(e.code, e.message);
  }
}
```
## What is DESIGN.md?

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/overview/

A design system document that AI agents read to generate consistent UI across your project.

Stitch

Every project has a visual identity: colors, fonts, spacing, component styles. Traditionally, this lives in a Figma file, a brand PDF, or a designer’s head. None of these are readable by an AI agent.

**`DESIGN.md` changes that.** It’s a plain-text design system document that both humans and agents can read, edit, and enforce. Think of it as the design counterpart to `AGENTS.md`:

| File | Who reads it | What it defines |
| --- | --- | --- |
| README.md | Humans | What the project is |
| AGENTS.md | Coding agents | How to build the project |
| DESIGN.md | Design agents | How the project should look and feel |

### What it gives you

Section titled “What it gives you”

When a design agent like Stitch reads your `DESIGN.md`, every screen it generates follows the same visual rules: your color palette, your typography, your component patterns. Without it, each screen stands alone. With it, they look like they belong together.

`DESIGN.md` is a **living artifact**, not a static config file. It evolves as your design evolves. The agent generates it, you refine it, and it’s re-applied to screens as you iterate.

Under the hood, every `DESIGN.md` has two layers: **YAML front matter** containing machine-readable design tokens (exact hex values, font properties, spacing scales) and a **markdown body** providing human-readable design rationale. Tokens give agents precise values. Prose tells them _why_ those values exist. See [the specification](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/specification/) for the full format.

### The philosophy

Section titled “The philosophy”

The DESIGN.md spec is a **foundation, not a prescription**. It provides a common ground that agents, tools, and teams can rely on — a shared vocabulary for colors, typography, layout, and components — while preserving the freedom to extend the format for domain-specific needs. Unknown sections and custom tokens are accepted, not rejected.

### How they’re created

Section titled “How they’re created”

There are three paths to a `DESIGN.md`, from effortless to precise.

Stitch

#### Let the agent generate it

Section titled “Let the agent generate it”

Describe the vibe. The agent translates your aesthetic intent into tokens and guidelines.

PROMPT

A playful coffee shop ordering app with warm colors, rounded corners, and a friendly feel

Stitch generates a complete design system (colors, typography, spacing, component styles) and summarizes it as a `DESIGN.md`.

#### Derive from branding

Section titled “Derive from branding”

If you already have a brand, provide a URL or image. The agent extracts your palette, typography, and style patterns to build the `DESIGN.md` from what already exists.

Stitch

#### Write it by hand

Section titled “Write it by hand”

Advanced users can author a `DESIGN.md` directly, encoding exact design preferences. Every section is just markdown with optional YAML front matter for design tokens. No special syntax beyond standard markdown and YAML.

### Example

Section titled “Example”

Below is a minimal `DESIGN.md` for a dark-themed productivity app. The YAML front matter defines the exact token values; the markdown body explains the design intent.

```
---
name: DevFocus Dark
colors:
  primary: "#2665fd"
  secondary: "#475569"
  surface: "#0b1326"
  on-surface: "#dae2fd"
  error: "#ffb4ab"
typography:
  body-md:
    fontFamily: Inter
    fontSize: 16px
    fontWeight: 400
rounded:
  md: 8px
---

# Design System

## Overview
A focused, minimal dark interface for a developer productivity tool.
Clean lines, low visual noise, high information density.

## Colors
- **Primary** (#2665fd): CTAs, active states, key interactive elements
- **Secondary** (#475569): Supporting UI, chips, secondary actions
- **Surface** (#0b1326): Page backgrounds
- **On-surface** (#dae2fd): Primary text on dark backgrounds
- **Error** (#ffb4ab): Validation errors, destructive actions

## Typography
- **Headlines**: Inter, semi-bold
- **Body**: Inter, regular, 14–16px
- **Labels**: Inter, medium, 12px, uppercase for section headers

## Components
- **Buttons**: Rounded (8px), primary uses brand blue fill
- **Inputs**: 1px border, subtle surface-variant background
- **Cards**: No elevation, relies on border and background contrast

## Do's and Don'ts
- Do use the primary color sparingly, only for the most important action
- Don't mix rounded and sharp corners in the same view
- Do maintain 4:1 contrast ratio for all text
```

This is what the agent reads when generating your next screen. For the complete format specification, see [The specification](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/specification/). To validate your DESIGN.md against the spec, see [Validate with the CLI](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/cli/).
## Import from your codebase

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/get-instructions/

Extract a DESIGN.md from an existing project — with a prompt, a skill, or both.

Your codebase already has a design language — colors scattered across stylesheets, spacing patterns buried in component files, typography choices locked in Tailwind configs. A `DESIGN.md` captures all of it in one place so Stitch can generate screens that look like they belong to your product instead of a blank-slate default.

There are two ways to get there: a quick prompt you can paste into any coding agent, or a dedicated skill that automates the entire pipeline.

### The quick prompt

Section titled “The quick prompt”

Copy this prompt into any coding agent (Gemini, Claude Code, Cursor, Antigravity) from a project directory. No skills or plugins required — the agent reads your source files and writes a `DESIGN.md` from what it finds.

PROMPT CONTEXT — OPTIONAL Add specifics about your codebase’s purpose, critical files, and goals. INSTRUCTIONS Read the codebase and/or website before designing. The repo and/or website are the source of truth. Start with real content. Pull product names, taglines, and copy from the README. Pull labels, values, and terminology from config files, CLI help text, schemas, and error messages. Nothing invented, nothing placeholder — if the repo doesn’t contain it, the design doesn’t show it. Look at existing code for visual identity: color values, type scales, spacing tokens, component patterns. If a design system exists, inherit it. If values are scattered across files, collect them — they reveal visual intent even when undocumented. Read the core logic and data structures, not just the docs. They tell you the product’s native shape — a timeline, a graph, a catalog, a pipeline. Let that shape organize the page instead of a section template. Find what the README leads with. That feature dominates the page. Establish its weight before placing anything else — what matters before what measures.

#### What the prompt does

Section titled “What the prompt does”

The prompt tells the agent to work backwards from your code, not forwards from a template. It extracts three layers:

1. **Content** — Product names, labels, and copy pulled directly from the source. No filler text, no lorem ipsum.
2. **Visual identity** — Colors, fonts, spacing, and component patterns gathered from stylesheets, theme files, and Tailwind configs.
3. **Information architecture** — The natural shape of your product’s data, which determines how the page is organized.

The output is a `DESIGN.md` you can drop into `.stitch/DESIGN.md` and immediately use for screen generation.

#### Tips for better results

Section titled “Tips for better results”

- **Point the agent at specific directories.** Add lines like “Focus on `src/styles/`, `tailwind.config.ts`, and `src/components/`” to the context block.
- **Name your stack.** Telling the agent “This is a React + Tailwind + shadcn/ui project” helps it look in the right places.
- **Iterate.** The first extraction captures the big picture. Refine it: “The accent color should be the teal from the navbar, not the blue from the footer.”

### Automated extraction with Stitch Design Skills

Section titled “Automated extraction with Stitch Design Skills”

The prompt above works anywhere, but it relies on the agent’s general reasoning. **Stitch Design Skills** are purpose-built agent instructions that know exactly where to look for design tokens in every major framework — React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, plain CSS, and Tailwind.

#### What are Stitch Design Skills?

Section titled “What are Stitch Design Skills?”

[Stitch Design Skills](https://github.com/google-labs-code/stitch-skills) is an open-source collection of 13 agent skills organized into three plugins:

| Plugin | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| stitch-design | Create and capture designs — extract tokens from code, snapshot running apps, upload to Stitch |
| stitch-build | Turn designs into code — React components, walkthrough videos, shadcn/ui integration |
| stitch-utilities | Enhance quality — prompt optimization, premium design systems, autonomous multi-page generation |

Skills follow the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/) open standard and work with any compatible coding agent.

#### Install the plugin suite

Section titled “Install the plugin suite”

```
npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope project --target claude-code
```

Replace `claude-code` with `cursor`, `gemini-cli`, or `antigravity` depending on your agent.

#### Extract a DESIGN.md from source code

Section titled “Extract a DESIGN.md from source code”

The `extract-design-md` skill scans your source tree without needing to build or run the application:

PROMPT

Extract the design system from ./src and write it to .stitch/DESIGN.md

The skill automatically detects your stack (Tailwind config, CSS custom properties, theme files, styled-components) and works through each design dimension:

- **Visual atmosphere** — Overall mood, whitespace philosophy, color temperature
- **Color palette** — Every unique color, deduplicated and assigned functional roles
- **Typography** — Font families, type scale hierarchy, weight and spacing patterns
- **Component styles** — Buttons, cards, navigation, inputs, and domain-specific elements
- **Layout principles** — Grid system, responsive breakpoints, spacing strategy

The output includes both YAML frontmatter (machine-readable tokens) and Markdown prose (human-readable design rationale). This bimodal format is what makes `DESIGN.md` work for both tools and AI agents.

#### Upload to Stitch

Section titled “Upload to Stitch”

Once you have a `DESIGN.md`, push it into a Stitch project so every generated screen follows your design system:

PROMPT

Upload .stitch/DESIGN.md to Stitch and create a design system from it.

The `manage-design-system` skill handles the upload and registers the design system at the project level. All future screens inherit your tokens automatically.

#### The full code-to-design pipeline

Section titled “The full code-to-design pipeline”

For a complete import — design system extraction, static HTML capture, and Stitch upload in one pass — use the orchestrator skill:

PROMPT

Upload the frontend at ./my-app into a Stitch project called “My App Migration”.

The `code-to-design` skill chains three steps: extract static HTML from the running app, reverse-engineer the design system from source, and upload everything to Stitch.

### Which method should I use?

Section titled “Which method should I use?”

| Situation | Recommended approach |
| --- | --- |
| Quick extraction, no setup | Copy the prompt above into any agent |
| Thorough, framework-aware extraction | Install skills, use extract-design-md |
| Full migration into Stitch | Install skills, use code-to-design |
| Writing a DESIGN.md from scratch | See What is DESIGN.md? for the format |
## The DESIGN.md specification

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/specification/

The formal specification for the DESIGN.md format — token schema, section structure, and type system.

A DESIGN.md file has two layers. The **YAML front matter** contains machine-readable design tokens — the precise values agents use to enforce consistency. The **markdown body** provides human-readable design rationale organized into `##` sections. Prose may use descriptive color names (e.g., “Midnight Forest Green”) that correspond to systematic token names (e.g., `primary`). The tokens are the normative values; the prose provides context for how to apply them.

The spec is a **foundation, not a prescription**. It provides common ground that agents, tools, and teams can rely on, while preserving the freedom to extend the format for domain-specific needs.

### Design tokens

Section titled “Design tokens”

DESIGN.md embeds design tokens as YAML front matter at the beginning of the file. The front matter block must begin with a line containing exactly `---` and end with a line containing exactly `---`. The YAML content between these delimiters follows the schema defined below.

The token system is inspired by the [W3C Design Token Format](https://www.designtokens.org/). Tokens are easily converted to and from `tokens.json`, Figma variables, and Tailwind theme configs.

```
---
version: alpha
name: Daylight Prestige
colors:
  primary: "#1A1C1E"
  secondary: "#6C7278"
  tertiary: "#B8422E"
typography:
  h1:
    fontFamily: Public Sans
    fontSize: 48px
    fontWeight: 600
    lineHeight: 1.1
    letterSpacing: -0.02em
rounded:
  sm: 4px
  md: 8px
spacing:
  sm: 8px
  md: 16px
components:
  button-primary:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.primary-60}"
    textColor: "{colors.primary-20}"
    rounded: "{rounded.md}"
    padding: 12px
---
```

#### Schema

Section titled “Schema”

```
version: <string>          # optional, current version: "alpha"
name: <string>
description: <string>      # optional
colors:
  <token-name>: <Color>
typography:
  <token-name>: <Typography>
rounded:
  <scale-level>: <Dimension>
spacing:
  <scale-level>: <Dimension | number>
components:
  <component-name>:
    <token-name>: <string | token reference>
```

The `<scale-level>` placeholder represents a named level in a sizing or spacing scale. Common level names include `xs`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, and `full`. Any descriptive string key is valid.

### Token types

Section titled “Token types”

| Type | Format | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Color | # + hex code (sRGB) | "#1A1C1E" |
| Dimension | number + unit (px, em, rem) | 48px, -0.02em |
| Token Reference | {path.to.token} | {colors.primary} |
| Typography | composite object | See properties below |

#### Typography properties

Section titled “Typography properties”

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fontFamily | string | The font family name |
| fontSize | Dimension | The font size |
| fontWeight | number | Numeric weight (e.g., 400, 700). In YAML, bare numbers and quoted strings are equivalent |
| lineHeight | Dimension \| number | A dimension (e.g., 24px) or a unitless multiplier (e.g., 1.6). Unitless is recommended |
| letterSpacing | Dimension | Letter spacing adjustment |
| fontFeature | string | Configures font-feature-settings |
| fontVariation | string | Configures font-variation-settings |

#### Token references

Section titled “Token references”

A token reference is wrapped in curly braces and contains an object path to another value in the YAML tree. For most token groups, the reference must point to a primitive value (e.g., `{colors.primary-60}`), not a group. Within the `components` section, references to composite values (e.g., `{typography.label-md}`) are permitted.

```
components:
  button-primary:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.primary-60}"
    textColor: "{colors.primary-20}"
    rounded: "{rounded.md}"
```

### Sections

Section titled “Sections”

Every DESIGN.md follows the same structure. Sections can be omitted if they are not relevant to the project, but those present should appear in the sequence listed below. All sections use `##` headings. An optional `#` heading may appear for document titling purposes but is not parsed as a section.

The section structure is intentionally open-ended. The canonical sections provide a shared vocabulary; design systems are free to add domain-specific sections beyond these.

#### Section order

Section titled “Section order”

| # | Section | Aliases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Overview | Brand & Style |
| 2 | Colors |  |
| 3 | Typography |  |
| 4 | Layout | Layout & Spacing |
| 5 | Elevation & Depth | Elevation |
| 6 | Shapes |  |
| 7 | Components |  |
| 8 | Do’s and Don’ts |  |

#### Overview

Section titled “Overview”

Also known as “Brand & Style.” A holistic description of the product’s look and feel. This section defines the brand personality, target audience, and the emotional response the UI should evoke. It serves as foundational context when a specific rule or token is not defined.

```
## Overview
A calm, professional interface for a healthcare scheduling platform.
Accessibility-first design with high contrast and generous touch targets.
```

#### Colors

Section titled “Colors”

Defines the color palettes for the design system. At least the `primary` palette should be defined. Additional palettes may be named freely; a common convention is `primary`, `secondary`, `tertiary`, and `neutral`.

```
## Colors

The palette is rooted in high-contrast neutrals and a single accent color.

- **Primary (#1A1C1E):** Deep ink for headlines and core text.
- **Secondary (#6C7278):** Sophisticated slate for borders, captions, metadata.
- **Tertiary (#B8422E):** The sole driver for interaction.
- **Neutral (#F7F5F2):** Warm limestone foundation.
```

**Design tokens:** A `map<string, Color>` mapping the token name to its hex value.

```
colors:
  primary: "#1A1C1E"
  secondary: "#6C7278"
  tertiary: "#B8422E"
  neutral: "#F7F5F2"
```

#### Typography

Section titled “Typography”

Defines typography levels. Most design systems have 9–15 levels, each with a semantic role (headline, body, label) and size variant (small, medium, large).

```
## Typography

- **Headlines:** Public Sans Semi-Bold for an institutional voice.
- **Body:** Public Sans Regular at 16px for long-form readability.
- **Labels:** Space Grotesk for technical data and metadata.
```

**Design tokens:** A `map<string, Typography>` mapping the token name to its typography properties.

```
typography:
  h1:
    fontFamily: Public Sans
    fontSize: 48px
    fontWeight: 600
    lineHeight: 1.1
    letterSpacing: -0.02em
  body-md:
    fontFamily: Public Sans
    fontSize: 16px
    fontWeight: 400
    lineHeight: 1.6
  label-caps:
    fontFamily: Space Grotesk
    fontSize: 12px
    fontWeight: 500
    lineHeight: 1
    letterSpacing: 0.1em
```

#### Layout

Section titled “Layout”

Also known as “Layout & Spacing.” Describes the layout and spacing strategy — grid models, spacing scales, and containment principles.

```
## Layout

The layout follows a Fluid Grid model for mobile and a Fixed-Max-Width
Grid for desktop (max 1200px). A strict 8px spacing scale is used.
```

**Design tokens:** A `map<string, Dimension | number>` mapping the spacing scale identifier to a dimension or unitless number (e.g., column counts or ratios).

```
spacing:
  base: 16px
  xs: 4px
  sm: 8px
  md: 16px
  lg: 32px
  xl: 64px
  gutter: 24px
  margin: 32px
```

#### Elevation & Depth

Section titled “Elevation & Depth”

Also known as “Elevation.” Describes how visual hierarchy is conveyed. For designs that use shadows, it defines the shadow properties. For flat designs, it explains the alternative methods (borders, tonal layers, color contrast).

```
## Elevation & Depth

Depth is achieved through tonal layers rather than heavy shadows.
Background uses a soft off-white; primary content sits on pure white cards.
```

#### Shapes

Section titled “Shapes”

Describes how visual elements are shaped — corner radii, edge treatments, and the overall shape language.

```
## Shapes

All interactive elements use a minimal 4px corner radius.
Modern enough to feel current, rigid enough to feel engineered.
```

**Design tokens:** A `map<string, Dimension>` mapping the scale level to the corner radius.

```
rounded:
  sm: 4px
  md: 8px
  lg: 12px
  full: 9999px
```

#### Components

Section titled “Components”

Style guidance for component atoms. The spec defines common component types — Buttons, Chips, Lists, Inputs, Checkboxes, Radio buttons, Tooltips — but design systems are encouraged to define additional components relevant to their domain.

```
## Components
- **Buttons**: Rounded (8px), primary uses brand blue fill, secondary uses outline
- **Inputs**: 1px border, surface-variant background, 12px padding
- **Cards**: No elevation, 1px outline border, 12px corner radius
```

**Design tokens:** A `map<string, map<string, string>>` mapping a component identifier to a group of sub-token properties. Token values may be literal values or references to previously defined tokens.

**Variants.** A component may have variants for different UI states (hover, active, pressed). Variants are defined as separate component entries with a related key name.

```
components:
  button-primary:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.primary-60}"
    textColor: "{colors.primary-20}"
    rounded: "{rounded.md}"
    padding: 12px
  button-primary-hover:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.primary-70}"
```

##### Component property tokens

Section titled “Component property tokens”

| Property | Type |
| --- | --- |
| backgroundColor | Color |
| textColor | Color |
| typography | Typography |
| rounded | Dimension |
| padding | Dimension |
| size | Dimension |
| height | Dimension |
| width | Dimension |

#### Do’s and Don’ts

Section titled “Do’s and Don’ts”

Practical guidelines and common pitfalls. These act as guardrails during generation.

```
## Do's and Don'ts

- Do use the primary color only for the single most important action per screen
- Don't mix rounded and sharp corners in the same view
- Do maintain WCAG AA contrast ratios (4.5:1 for normal text)
- Don't use more than two font weights on a single screen
```

### Consumer behavior for unknown content

Section titled “Consumer behavior for unknown content”

The spec is designed to be extended. When a consumer encounters content not defined by this specification:

| Scenario | Behavior | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown section heading | Preserve; do not error | ## Iconography |
| Unknown color token name | Accept if value is valid | surface-container-high: '#ede7dd' |
| Unknown typography token name | Accept as valid typography | telemetry-data |
| Unknown spacing value | Accept; store as string if not a valid dimension | grid-columns: '5' |
| Unknown component property | Accept with warning | borderColor |
| Duplicate section heading | Error; reject the file | Two ## Colors headings |

### Recommended token names

Section titled “Recommended token names”

The following names are commonly used across design systems. They are not required but are provided as guidance for consistency.

**Colors:** `primary`, `secondary`, `tertiary`, `neutral`, `surface`, `on-surface`, `error`

**Typography:** `headline-display`, `headline-lg`, `headline-md`, `body-lg`, `body-md`, `body-sm`, `label-lg`, `label-md`, `label-sm`

**Rounded:** `none`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, `full`
## View, edit, and export

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/usage/

Work with your design system in the Stitch UI. View tokens, tweak values, and export with your project.

### View the design system

Section titled “View the design system”

Open the **Design System** panel to see the active design system for any screen. The panel shows the resolved tokens: colors, fonts, roundedness, spacing, and component patterns.

If the project has multiple design systems, the panel displays the one applied to the currently selected screen.

### Set a default design system

Section titled “Set a default design system”

To apply a design system to all future screens in a project, select it as the project default. New screens generated after this point will automatically inherit its tokens.

Existing screens are not retroactively updated. To bring them into alignment, apply the design system to them individually.

### Edit via the Design System panel

Section titled “Edit via the Design System panel”

The Design System panel supports direct edits to the active design system. Changes you make here update both the structured tokens and the `DESIGN.md` summary.

Editable properties include:

- **Color palette**: primary, secondary, tertiary, and neutral base colors
- **Typography**: headline, body, and label font families
- **Roundedness**: corner radius scale

For more granular changes (component guidelines, do’s and don’ts, or the overview narrative), edit the `DESIGN.md` markdown directly.

### Export with your project

Section titled “Export with your project”

When you export a project, the `DESIGN.md` file is included in the zip alongside the generated screens. This gives downstream consumers (developers, other design tools, or other agents) a portable record of the design system.

The exported `DESIGN.md` is a standalone document. It doesn’t depend on Stitch to be useful.

### Working outside Stitch?

Section titled “Working outside Stitch?”

The [`@google/design.md` CLI](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/cli/) validates any DESIGN.md file against the formal spec, checks WCAG contrast ratios, and exports tokens to Tailwind or W3C Design Token formats. It works with any DESIGN.md, whether it was generated by Stitch or written by hand.
## Validate with the CLI

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/cli/

Lint, diff, and export DESIGN.md files using the @google/design.md command-line tool.

The `@google/design.md` CLI validates your design system against the spec, catches broken token references, checks WCAG contrast ratios, and exports tokens to other formats — all as structured JSON that agents can act on.

### Install

Section titled “Install”

```
npm install @google/design.md
```

Or run directly without installing:

```
npx @google/design.md lint DESIGN.md
```

All commands accept a file path or `-` for stdin. Output defaults to JSON.

### Lint a DESIGN.md

Section titled “Lint a DESIGN.md”

Validate a DESIGN.md file for structural correctness. The linter parses the YAML front matter, resolves all token references, runs [8 lint rules](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/linting-rules/), and reports findings.

```
npx @google/design.md lint DESIGN.md
```

Example output:

```
{
  "findings": [
    {
      "severity": "warning",
      "path": "colors",
      "message": "No 'primary' color defined. The agent will auto-generate key colors, reducing your control over the palette."
    },
    {
      "severity": "info",
      "message": "Design system defines 4 colors, 3 typography scales, 2 rounding levels."
    }
  ],
  "summary": { "errors": 0, "warnings": 1, "infos": 1 }
}
```

Pipe from stdin if you’re generating DESIGN.md files programmatically:

```
cat DESIGN.md | npx @google/design.md lint -
```

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| file | positional | required | Path to DESIGN.md (or - for stdin) |
| --format | json \| text | json | Output format |

Exit code `1` if errors are found, `0` otherwise.

### Compare two versions

Section titled “Compare two versions”

Detect token-level changes between two DESIGN.md files. The `diff` command reports which tokens were added, removed, or modified, and flags regressions (more errors or warnings in the “after” file).

```
npx @google/design.md diff DESIGN.md DESIGN-v2.md
```

Example output:

```
{
  "tokens": {
    "colors": { "added": ["accent"], "removed": [], "modified": ["tertiary"] },
    "typography": { "added": [], "removed": [], "modified": [] }
  },
  "findings": {
    "before": { "errors": 0, "warnings": 1 },
    "after": { "errors": 0, "warnings": 2 },
    "delta": { "errors": 0, "warnings": 1 }
  },
  "regression": true
}
```

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| before | positional | required | Path to the “before” DESIGN.md |
| after | positional | required | Path to the “after” DESIGN.md |
| --format | json \| text | json | Output format |

Exit code `1` if regressions are detected.

### Export tokens

Section titled “Export tokens”

Convert DESIGN.md tokens to other formats for use in your codebase.

#### Tailwind CSS

Section titled “Tailwind CSS”

Generate a `theme.extend` configuration object:

```
npx @google/design.md export --format tailwind DESIGN.md
```

The output is a JSON object with `colors`, `fontFamily`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`, and `spacing` mapped from your design tokens. Drop it into your `tailwind.config.js`.

#### DTCG (W3C Design Tokens)

Section titled “DTCG (W3C Design Tokens)”

Generate a [W3C Design Tokens Format Module](https://tr.designtokens.org/format/) compliant `tokens.json`:

```
npx @google/design.md export --format dtcg DESIGN.md
```

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| file | positional | required | Path to DESIGN.md |
| --format | tailwind \| dtcg | required | Export target format |

### View the spec

Section titled “View the spec”

Output the DESIGN.md format specification. This is useful for injecting spec context into agent prompts so the agent knows exactly what structure to produce.

```
npx @google/design.md spec
npx @google/design.md spec --rules
npx @google/design.md spec --rules-only --format json
```

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| --rules | boolean | false | Append the active linting rules table |
| --rules-only | boolean | false | Output only the linting rules table |
| --format | markdown \| json | markdown | Output format |

### Programmatic API

Section titled “Programmatic API”

The linter is also available as a TypeScript library:

```
import { lint } from '@google/design.md/linter';

const report = lint(markdownString);

console.log(report.findings);      // Finding[]
console.log(report.summary);       // { errors, warnings, infos }
console.log(report.designSystem);  // Resolved DesignSystemState
console.log(report.tailwindConfig); // Generated Tailwind theme
```
## Linting rules

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/linting-rules/

The 8 rules the DESIGN.md linter enforces, what triggers each one, and how to resolve findings.

The `@google/design.md` linter runs rules against a parsed DESIGN.md file. Each rule produces findings at a fixed severity level: **error** (exit code 1), **warning**, or **info**.

### broken-ref

Section titled “broken-ref”

**Severity:** error

Detects token references (`{path.to.token}`) that do not resolve to any defined token in the YAML front matter. Also flags unknown component sub-token property names.

**Triggers when:**

- A component references a token path that does not exist (e.g., `{colors.accent}` when no `accent` color is defined)
- A component uses a property name not in the recognized set (`backgroundColor`, `textColor`, `typography`, `rounded`, `padding`, `size`, `height`, `width`)

**Example finding:**

```
error  components.button-primary  Reference {colors.accent} does not resolve to any defined token.
```

**Resolution:** Define the missing token in the YAML front matter, or correct the reference path. For unknown properties, use one of the recognized component sub-token names.

### missing-primary

Section titled “missing-primary”

**Severity:** warning

Warns when colors are defined in the front matter but no token named `primary` exists. Without a primary color, agents will auto-generate one, reducing your control over the palette.

**Triggers when:** The `colors` section has one or more entries, but none is named `primary`.

**Example finding:**

```
warning  colors  No 'primary' color defined. The agent will auto-generate key colors, reducing your control over the palette.
```

**Resolution:** Add a `primary` entry to the `colors` section.

### contrast-ratio

Section titled “contrast-ratio”

**Severity:** warning

Checks WCAG contrast ratios for component `backgroundColor` and `textColor` pairs. Warns when the ratio falls below the AA minimum of 4.5:1.

**Triggers when:** A component defines both `backgroundColor` and `textColor`, and the resolved color values produce a contrast ratio below 4.5:1.

**Example finding:**

```
warning  components.card-dark  textColor (#999999) on backgroundColor (#333333) has contrast ratio 3.48:1, below WCAG AA minimum of 4.5:1.
```

**Resolution:** Adjust either the background or text color to meet the 4.5:1 minimum ratio.

### orphaned-tokens

Section titled “orphaned-tokens”

**Severity:** warning

Identifies color tokens that are defined but never referenced by any component. Orphaned tokens add noise and may indicate an incomplete design system.

**Triggers when:** A color token exists in the `colors` section but is not referenced by any component’s properties. Only fires when at least one component is defined.

**Example finding:**

```
warning  colors.tertiary  'tertiary' is defined but never referenced by any component.
```

**Resolution:** Reference the token in a component, or remove it if it is no longer needed.

### missing-typography

Section titled “missing-typography”

**Severity:** warning

Warns when colors are defined but no typography tokens exist. Without typography tokens, agents will fall back to their own font choices.

**Triggers when:** The `colors` section has entries but the `typography` section is empty.

**Example finding:**

```
warning  typography  No typography tokens defined. Agents will use default font choices, reducing your control over the design system's typographic identity.
```

**Resolution:** Add at least one typography token (e.g., `body-md`) to the front matter.

### section-order

Section titled “section-order”

**Severity:** warning

Warns when markdown sections appear out of the [canonical order](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/specification/#section-order) defined by the spec. The expected sequence is: Overview, Colors, Typography, Layout, Elevation & Depth, Shapes, Components, Do’s and Don’ts.

**Triggers when:** A recognized section heading appears before another recognized section that should precede it. Section aliases (e.g., “Elevation” for “Elevation & Depth”) are resolved before checking.

**Example finding:**

```
warning  Section 'Components' appears before 'Typography', which is out of order. Expected order: Overview, Colors, Typography, Layout, Elevation & Depth, Shapes, Components, Do's and Don'ts
```

**Resolution:** Reorder the sections in the markdown body to match the canonical sequence.

### missing-sections

Section titled “missing-sections”

**Severity:** info

Notes when optional token sections (`spacing`, `rounded`) are absent from a file that already defines other tokens. These sections are not required, but their absence means agents will fall back to defaults.

**Triggers when:** The `colors` section has entries but `spacing` or `rounded` has no entries.

**Example finding:**

```
info  spacing  No 'spacing' section defined. Layout spacing will fall back to agent defaults.
```

**Resolution:** Add a `spacing` or `rounded` section to the front matter if you want explicit control over those values.

### token-summary

Section titled “token-summary”

**Severity:** info

Emits a summary diagnostic reporting how many tokens are defined in each section. This is purely informational.

**Example finding:**

```
info  Design system defines 4 colors, 3 typography scales, 2 rounding levels, 6 spacing tokens, 3 components.
```

### Summary

Section titled “Summary”

| Rule | Severity | What it checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| broken-ref | error | Token references that don’t resolve; unknown component sub-tokens |
| missing-primary | warning | Colors defined but no primary exists |
| contrast-ratio | warning | Component backgroundColor/textColor below WCAG AA 4.5:1 |
| orphaned-tokens | warning | Color tokens defined but never referenced by a component |
| missing-typography | warning | Colors defined but no typography tokens exist |
| section-order | warning | Sections out of canonical order |
| missing-sections | info | Optional sections (spacing, rounded) absent |
| token-summary | info | Count of tokens defined per section |
## Get started with Agent Skills

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/skills/get-started/

Install the Stitch Design Skills, connect to the MCP server, and generate your first screen — all from your coding agent.

Stitch Design Skills are agent instructions that extend your coding agent with design superpowers — generating screens, extracting design systems, building multi-page sites, and converting designs to React components. They work with any agent that supports the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/) standard: Gemini CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, or Antigravity.

### Install the plugin suite

Section titled “Install the plugin suite”

Run this from your project directory:

```
npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope project --target claude-code
```

This installs all three plugins (`stitch-design`, `stitch-build`, `stitch-utilities`) with 13 skills total.

#### Pick your agent target

Section titled “Pick your agent target”

```
# Claude Code
npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope project --target claude-code

# Cursor
npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope project --target cursor

# Gemini CLI
npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope project --target gemini-cli

# Antigravity
npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope project --target antigravity
```

#### Install selectively (optional)

Section titled “Install selectively (optional)”

If you only need specific skills:

```
npx skills add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --skills stitch::generate-design
```

> Many skills depend on each other. The `code-to-design` skill, for example, requires `extract-static-html`, `extract-design-md`, and `upload-to-stitch`. The full plugin install is the safer choice.

### Connect the Stitch MCP server

Section titled “Connect the Stitch MCP server”

The skills talk to Stitch through the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/). Follow the [Stitch MCP Setup Instructions](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/mcp/setup/) to register the server and configure your API credentials.

Once connected, your agent gains access to tools like `list_projects`, `generate_screen_from_text`, and `get_screen`.

#### Verify the connection

Section titled “Verify the connection”

PROMPT

List my Stitch projects.

You should see your existing projects — or an empty list if this is your first time using Stitch. If you see an error, double-check that the MCP server is running and your API key is valid.

### Generate your first screen

Section titled “Generate your first screen”

Start with a rough idea. The `enhance-prompt` skill transforms vague concepts into structured, generation-ready prompts.

PROMPT

Enhance this prompt for Stitch: “Create a landing page for an artisanal coffee shop”

Notice the output — the skill adds a platform specification, structures the page into numbered sections, replaces vague terms with specific UI/UX keywords, and generates a design system block with color roles. This enhanced prompt produces dramatically better results than the original.

Now generate:

PROMPT

Generate a screen in my Stitch project using the enhanced prompt from the previous step.

This takes 15–30 seconds. When complete, you’ll see a confirmation with the screen ID and file paths. Open the generated screenshot to see your design — a complete landing page with hero section, feature cards, navigation, and footer, all from a single text prompt.

### What’s next

Section titled “What’s next”

You’ve installed skills, connected to Stitch, and generated your first screen. Here’s where to go from here:

- **[Import from your codebase](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/get-instructions/)** — Extract a DESIGN.md from existing source code
- **[Code to Design roundtrip](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/skills/roundtrip/)** — Import a React app into Stitch, edit the design, export back to components
- **[Build in a loop](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/skills/build-in-a-loop/)** — Generate an entire website from a single concept
- **[Skill reference](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/skills/reference/)** — Full catalog of all 13 skills

### Troubleshooting

Section titled “Troubleshooting”

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| npx plugins not found | Install Node.js 18+: node --version |
| MCP server not responding | Verify setup: MCP Setup guide |
| Skills not visible in agent | Restart the agent session after installation |
| Permission errors | Use --scope project instead of --scope global |
| API key errors | Confirm the key in your agent’s MCP config hasn’t expired |
## Code to Design roundtrip

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/skills/roundtrip/

Import a React app into Stitch, edit the design visually, and export updated components — the full roundtrip.

The roundtrip workflow connects your codebase and Stitch in both directions. Start from a React app, extract its design system and screens into Stitch, make visual edits in the cloud, and export the updated designs back to clean React components.

### What you’ll build

Section titled “What you’ll build”

Starting from an existing React + Vite application, you’ll extract design tokens, capture screens as static HTML, upload everything to Stitch, edit the design, and convert it back to React components.

#### Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”

- Completed [Get started with skills](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/agent-skills/get-started/) (skills installed, MCP connected)
- An existing React application with a working dev server
- Node.js 18+ and `puppeteer` installed

### Step 1: Extract design tokens from source

Section titled “Step 1: Extract design tokens from source”

Scan your source files to reverse-engineer a design system document — no build step required.

PROMPT

Extract the design system from ./my-app/src and write it to .stitch/DESIGN.md

The `extract-design-md` skill reads your components, stylesheets, Tailwind config, and theme files. It identifies colors, typography, spacing, and component patterns.

Open the resulting `.stitch/DESIGN.md` and you’ll see:

- **YAML frontmatter** with machine-readable color tokens
- **Markdown sections** describing visual atmosphere, palette, typography, and layout
- **Descriptive names** like “Deep Ocean Blue (#1a365d)” instead of raw hex codes

### Step 2: Capture static HTML snapshots

Section titled “Step 2: Capture static HTML snapshots”

Start your dev server, then capture the running app as self-contained HTML:

PROMPT

Extract static HTML from [http://localhost:5173](http://localhost:5173/) and save to .stitch/designs/home.html

The skill launches headless Chrome, captures the fully rendered DOM, inlines all CSS, and converts images to base64 data URIs. Each output file is completely self-contained — no external dependencies.

For multiple pages, repeat for each route:

PROMPT

Also extract [http://localhost:5173/about](http://localhost:5173/about) to .stitch/designs/about.html

### Step 3: Upload to Stitch

Section titled “Step 3: Upload to Stitch”

Push everything to a new Stitch project in one command:

PROMPT

Upload .stitch/DESIGN.md and all HTML files in .stitch/designs/ to a new Stitch project called “My App Migration”

The skill creates a project, uploads the DESIGN.md as a design system, and imports each HTML file as a screen. Open [Stitch](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/) to see your project with all the uploaded screens, styled according to your design system.

### Step 4: Edit the design

Section titled “Step 4: Edit the design”

Make targeted visual changes without touching code:

PROMPT

Edit the home screen: add a testimonial section between the features and the footer with three customer quotes in a horizontal card layout.

The skill calls `edit_screens` with your instruction while preserving the existing design system. One change at a time produces the best results — iterate with additional edits rather than bundling everything into one prompt.

### Step 5: Export back to React

Section titled “Step 5: Export back to React”

Convert the updated Stitch screens back to component code:

PROMPT

Convert the screens in my Stitch project to React components.

The `react-components` skill downloads the latest screen HTML, extracts Tailwind theme values, breaks the design into modular components, creates type-safe interfaces, moves static data into `src/data/mockData.ts`, and validates everything via AST.

Start your dev server — the React components now reflect the design changes you made in Stitch, including the new testimonial section.

### The full roundtrip

Section titled “The full roundtrip”

Here’s what you just completed:

| Step | Direction | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Extract tokens | Code → DESIGN.md | Reverse-engineered the design system from source |
| Capture HTML | Code → Static files | Snapshot the running app as self-contained HTML |
| Upload | Files → Stitch | Imported assets and design system to the cloud |
| Edit | Stitch → Updated design | Made targeted visual changes |
| Export | Stitch → React | Generated updated components from the design |

### What’s next

Section titled “What’s next”

- **[Import from your codebase](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/get-instructions/)** — More options for extracting design systems, including a quick prompt that needs no skills
- **[Create a premium design system](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/agent-skills/premium-design-system/)** — Generate a curated design system with anti-generic standards
- **[Why semantic tokens?](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/agent-skills/semantic-tokens/)** — Understand why descriptive design language works better for AI than raw CSS
## Build in a loop

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/skills/build-in-a-loop/

The stitch-loop autonomous build cycle generates entire websites page by page. Define the vision and design system once — the skill handles the rest.

The `stitch-loop` skill generates entire websites page by page, automatically. You define the vision and design system upfront. The skill handles the rest — generating each page, wiring navigation, and queuing the next task.

### How the baton loop works

Section titled “How the baton loop works”

A relay baton file at `.stitch/next-prompt.md` defines the current page to generate. After each page, the skill updates the baton with the next task. This creates a self-sustaining build cycle.

**State files the skill manages:**

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| .stitch/next-prompt.md | Current task (the baton) |
| .stitch/SITE.md | Site vision, sitemap, and roadmap |
| .stitch/DESIGN.md | Design system for visual consistency |
| .stitch/metadata.json | Stitch project and screen IDs |

### Step 1: Define the site vision

Section titled “Step 1: Define the site vision”

Create `.stitch/SITE.md` describing your site:

```
# Site: Artisan Coffee Co.

## Vision
A 5-page portfolio website for a specialty coffee roaster.

## Sitemap
- [ ] index — Landing page with hero and featured blends
- [ ] about — Origin story and roasting philosophy
- [ ] menu — Coffee menu with categories and pricing
- [ ] locations — Store locations with map
- [ ] contact — Contact form and hours
```

### Step 2: Establish a design system

Section titled “Step 2: Establish a design system”

Set visual consistency before generating any pages. The preferred approach — generate a premium design system:

PROMPT

Generate a DESIGN.md for an artisanal coffee brand using the taste-design skill. Warm tones, editorial typography, generous whitespace.

Or extract from an existing codebase:

PROMPT

Extract the design system from ./existing-site/src into .stitch/DESIGN.md

### Step 3: Write the first baton

Section titled “Step 3: Write the first baton”

Create `.stitch/next-prompt.md` for the first page:

```
---
page: index
---
A warm, editorial landing page for Artisan Coffee Co.

**DESIGN SYSTEM (REQUIRED):**
[Paste from .stitch/DESIGN.md]

**Page Structure:**
1. Header with logo and navigation links to about, menu, locations, contact
2. Hero section with full-width image, headline, and primary CTA
3. Featured blends section with three product cards
4. Testimonial section with customer quote
5. Footer with address, social links, and copyright
```

### Step 4: Run the loop

Section titled “Step 4: Run the loop”

PROMPT

Read .stitch/next-prompt.md and execute the stitch-loop build cycle.

The skill generates the screen via Stitch, downloads HTML and screenshots, moves the HTML to `site/public/`, updates the sitemap, and writes the next baton. Repeat the same prompt for each subsequent page — the baton drives the cycle forward.

### Navigation and consistency

Section titled “Navigation and consistency”

The skill automatically wires internal links across pages, adds new pages to the global navigation, and maintains consistent headers and footers.

If navigation drifts after several pages:

PROMPT

Update all page headers to include links to: index, about, menu, locations, contact.

### Tips for better results

Section titled “Tips for better results”

- **Edit rather than regenerate.** If a page is close but not right, targeted edits preserve more context than starting over.
- **Check the design system.** Visual drift usually means the DESIGN.md wasn’t included in the prompt.
- **Compare screenshots.** After generating multiple pages, ask the agent to compare them for visual consistency.

### Orchestration options

Section titled “Orchestration options”

| Method | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| Manual | Run the agent repeatedly with the same prompt |
| Human-in-loop | Review each page before continuing |
| CI/CD | Trigger on .stitch/next-prompt.md changes |
| Agent chains | One agent dispatches to another via the baton file |
## Generate walkthrough videos

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/skills/walkthrough-videos/

Create professional walkthrough videos from Stitch project screens using Remotion with animated transitions.

The `remotion` skill turns your Stitch project screens into polished walkthrough videos — complete with cross-fade transitions, spring-animated zoom effects, and text overlays. Useful for demos, stakeholder reviews, or documentation.

### Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”

- A Stitch project with at least 2 designed screens
- Node.js and npm installed
- Access to the Stitch MCP server

### Retrieve screens

Section titled “Retrieve screens”

PROMPT

List all screens in Stitch project projects/123456 and download their screenshots.

The skill fetches screen metadata via MCP, downloads full-resolution screenshots to `assets/screens/`, and creates a `screens.json` manifest with titles, dimensions, and per-screen durations.

### Set up and generate

Section titled “Set up and generate”

If no Remotion project exists, the skill creates one. Then configure your transitions:

#### Fade (default)

Section titled “Fade (default)”

Smooth cross-fades between screens. Best for calm, professional presentations.

PROMPT

Use fade transitions between all screens with 15 frames overlap.

#### Slide

Section titled “Slide”

Directional slides for sequential user flows:

PROMPT

Use slide transitions from left to right to show the user journey.

#### Zoom

Section titled “Zoom”

Spring-animated zoom effects for emphasizing specific features:

PROMPT

Add a zoom-in effect on the hero section of the home screen before transitioning to the features page.

Mix and match — use fades for most screens and a zoom to highlight a key moment.

### Add text overlays

Section titled “Add text overlays”

#### Screen titles

Section titled “Screen titles”

PROMPT

Add the screen title as a bottom overlay on each slide, fading in after 0.5 seconds.

#### Feature callouts

Section titled “Feature callouts”

PROMPT

Add a pulsing circle highlighting the search bar on the navigation screen.

#### Progress indicator

Section titled “Progress indicator”

PROMPT

Add a thin progress bar at the top showing the current position in the walkthrough.

### Render the video

Section titled “Render the video”

Preview first in the browser-based Remotion Studio:

PROMPT

Start the Remotion Studio to preview the walkthrough video.

Then render to file:

PROMPT

Render the walkthrough video as walkthrough.mp4 with H.264 codec.

#### Quality options

Section titled “Quality options”

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| --quality 100 | Maximum quality (larger file) |
| --codec h264 | Best compatibility |
| --codec h265 | Better compression, less compatibility |
| --concurrency 4 | Parallel rendering for speed |

### Adjusting pacing

Section titled “Adjusting pacing”

- **Too fast?** Increase per-screen duration in `screens.json` (default is 3–5 seconds)
- **Too slow?** Reduce duration or add more dynamic transitions
- **Uneven?** Set longer durations for complex screens, shorter for simple ones

PROMPT

Set the dashboard screen duration to 6 seconds and the login screen to 3 seconds.

### Troubleshooting

Section titled “Troubleshooting”

| Issue | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Blurry screenshots | Append =w{width} to download URLs for full resolution |
| Choppy animations | Increase frame rate to 60fps |
| Misaligned text overlays | Match composition dimensions to screen dimensions |
| Remotion build fails | Check Node version compatibility; run npm install |
## Taste

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/skills/taste/

Generate a DESIGN.md that actively prevents generic AI aesthetics — calibrated color, distinctive typography, and explicit anti-patterns.

This excellent Agent Skill was contributed by a community member, Leon Lin.

Leonxlnx / taste-skill Star

Portable Agent Skills that upgrade AI-built interfaces: stronger layout, typography, motion, and spacing

Markdown Leonxlnx/taste-skill

Most AI-generated interfaces converge on the same look: oversaturated purple gradients, centered three-column cards, `Inter` font, fabricated statistics. The `taste-design` skill generates design systems that explicitly ban these patterns and enforce premium standards.

### When to use taste-design

Section titled “When to use taste-design”

| Skill | What it does | Philosophy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| extract-design-md | Reverse-engineers tokens from source code | Descriptive — documents what exists |
| design-md | Extracts tokens from existing Stitch screens | Descriptive — documents what exists |
| taste-design | Generates a design system from a concept | Prescriptive — enforces premium standards |

Use `taste-design` when starting fresh and you want a design system that stands above the AI-generated average.

### Generate a premium DESIGN.md

Section titled “Generate a premium DESIGN.md”

PROMPT

Generate a premium DESIGN.md for a high-density financial analytics dashboard using the taste-design skill.

The output includes visual atmosphere calibrated on the taste spectrum, strict anti-pattern rules, calibrated color science, opinionated typography, and spring-physics motion specifications.

### Color calibration

Section titled “Color calibration”

Colors use HSL with intentionally restrained saturation. This reflects a principle from print design: sophisticated palettes use low-saturation colors for large surfaces and reserve high saturation for small, intentional accents.

**Rules the skill enforces:**

- Accent saturation stays below 80% — no oversaturated neon
- Pure black (`#000000`) is banned — use off-blacks like Zinc-950 (`#18181B`)
- Maximum one accent color — forces visual discipline

#### Adjusting the palette

Section titled “Adjusting the palette”

PROMPT

Adjust the DESIGN.md accent color to a deep teal (#0D9488) and warm the neutrals toward sand tones.

### Typography

Section titled “Typography”

The skill uses musical interval ratios for the type scale — the same harmonic relationships that make musical intervals sound natural:

| Scale | Ratio | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minor Third | 1.200 | Compact, information-dense |
| Major Third | 1.250 | Balanced, versatile |
| Perfect Fourth | 1.333 | Generous, editorial |
| Golden Ratio | 1.618 | Dramatic, high-impact |

**Font pairing rules:**

- `Inter` is banned in premium contexts — too ubiquitous
- Recommended sans-serif: `Geist`, `Outfit`, `Cabinet Grotesk`, `Satoshi`
- Recommended modern serif: `Fraunces`, `Gambarino`, `Editorial New`
- Dashboard constraint: sans-serif + monospace only (`Geist` + `Geist Mono`)

PROMPT

Use Outfit for display headlines and Geist for body text with Geist Mono for data.

### Spatial rhythm

Section titled “Spatial rhythm”

Every margin, padding, and gap is a multiple of the base unit (typically 4px or 8px). This creates spatial relationships the eye perceives as orderly even when asymmetric.

#### Adjusting density

Section titled “Adjusting density”

The taste spectrum ranges from 1 (airy) to 10 (cockpit-dense):

PROMPT

Generate a DESIGN.md at density 8 — this is a monitoring dashboard that needs to display many metrics simultaneously.

Higher density triggers monospace numbers for alignment, border-top dividers instead of cards, tighter spacing ratios, and flat surfaces distinguished by typography rather than shadow.

### The taste scoring rubric

Section titled “The taste scoring rubric”

Evaluate your DESIGN.md across four dimensions. A premium design scores 7+ across all four:

| Dimension | What it measures |
| --- | --- |
| Color Sophistication | Palette restraint, saturation discipline, contrast intentionality |
| Typographic Craft | Font distinctiveness, scale harmony, weight hierarchy |
| Spatial Coherence | Base unit consistency, rhythm, responsive scaling |
| Visual Hierarchy | Clear primary/secondary/tertiary levels, information architecture |

If any dimension feels weak:

PROMPT

The typographic hierarchy feels flat. Increase the weight contrast between headlines and body, and add letter-spacing differentiation.

### Anti-pattern checklist

Section titled “Anti-pattern checklist”

Before finalizing, verify these are absent:

- ❌ No emojis in the design
- ❌ No `Inter` font
- ❌ No pure black (`#000000`)
- ❌ No neon outer glow shadows
- ❌ No 3-column equal card layouts
- ❌ No fabricated metrics (“99.98% UPTIME”, “124ms AVG. RESPONSE”)
- ❌ No AI copywriting clichés (“Elevate”, “Seamless”, “Unleash”)
- ❌ No filler UI text (“Scroll to explore”, bouncing chevrons)
- ❌ No `LABEL // YEAR` formatting patterns
## Skill reference

Source: https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/skills/reference/

All Stitch Skills — what they do, which tools they use, and how to invoke them.

The Stitch Design Skills are organized into three plugins. Each skill follows the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/) open standard and works with any compatible coding agent.

### stitch-design

Section titled “stitch-design”

Core design workflows for creating, capturing, and managing designs.

#### code-to-design

Section titled “code-to-design”

Orchestrates the full import pipeline: detect framework → extract static HTML → extract design tokens → upload to Stitch.

PROMPT

Upload the frontend at ./dashboard into Stitch project “Dashboard Migration”.

**Dependencies:** `extract-static-html`, `extract-design-md`, `upload-to-stitch`

#### generate-design

Section titled “generate-design”

Generates new screens from text or images, edits existing screens, and creates design variants.

PROMPT

Make a browse tab for a mobile dating app with card-based profiles.

**MCP tools:** `generate_screen_from_text`, `edit_screens`, `generate_variants`, `list_projects`, `create_project`, `list_design_systems`

#### manage-design-system

Section titled “manage-design-system”

Uploads DESIGN.md specifications, creates project-level design systems, and applies them to screens.

PROMPT

Upload .stitch/DESIGN.md and create a design system for project 123456.

**MCP tools:** `create_design_system_from_design_md`, `apply_design_system`, `list_design_systems`, `upload_design_md`

#### extract-design-md

Section titled “extract-design-md”

Reverse-engineers a `DESIGN.md` from frontend source code — React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, plain CSS, or Tailwind. No build step required.

PROMPT

Extract the design system from ./my-app/src and write it to .stitch/DESIGN.md

**Pipeline:** Scan source tree → Detect framework → Extract tokens → Normalize → Deduplicate → Generate DESIGN.md

#### extract-static-html

Section titled “extract-static-html”

Captures self-contained HTML snapshots from running web applications, inlining CSS and converting images to base64.

PROMPT

Extract a static snapshot of [http://localhost:5173](http://localhost:5173/) and save to .stitch/home.html

#### upload-to-stitch

Section titled “upload-to-stitch”

Uploads local assets (images, HTML) to the Stitch REST API via a standalone script that bypasses LLM output token limits.

PROMPT

Upload landing_page.html to Stitch project projects/987654321.

### stitch-build

Section titled “stitch-build”

Code generation and media compilation from Stitch designs.

#### react-components

Section titled “react-components”

Converts Stitch screens to modular React component hierarchies with Tailwind theme extraction and AST-based validation.

PROMPT

Convert all screens in project projects/123 to React components.

#### remotion

Section titled “remotion”

Generates walkthrough videos from Stitch projects using Remotion with spring-animated zoom effects and configurable transitions. See [Generate walkthrough videos](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/agent-skills/walkthrough-videos/).

PROMPT

Create a walkthrough video of the Calculator App Stitch project.

#### shadcn-ui

Section titled “shadcn-ui”

Expert guidance for integrating shadcn/ui components — discovery, installation, and customization with Radix UI and Tailwind CSS.

PROMPT

Set up shadcn/ui and build a data table with sorting and pagination.

### stitch-utilities

Section titled “stitch-utilities”

Quality enhancement at both ends of the pipeline.

#### design-md

Section titled “design-md”

Analyzes existing Stitch project screens and synthesizes a `DESIGN.md` from the rendered output. This is the _design → tokens_ direction (as opposed to `extract-design-md` which is _code → tokens_).

PROMPT

Analyze Stitch project 123456 and generate a DESIGN.md capturing its visual identity.

**MCP tools:** `list_screens`, `get_screen`, `upload_design_md`, `list_projects`, `get_project`

#### enhance-prompt

Section titled “enhance-prompt”

Transforms vague ideas into structured, generation-ready prompts with UI/UX keywords, design system context, and page structure.

PROMPT

Enhance this prompt: “make a settings page”

#### stitch-loop

Section titled “stitch-loop”

Orchestrates autonomous multi-page site generation using a relay baton pattern. See [Build a multi-page site](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/agent-skills/multi-page-site/).

PROMPT

Read .stitch/next-prompt.md and execute the stitch-loop build cycle.

#### taste-design

Section titled “taste-design”

Generates premium `DESIGN.md` files with anti-generic standards — calibrated color science, musical-interval type scales, spring physics motion, and an explicit anti-pattern catalog. See [Create a premium design system](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/agent-skills/premium-design-system/).

PROMPT

Generate a premium DESIGN.md for a high-density financial analytics cockpit.

### Installing individual skills

Section titled “Installing individual skills”

The full plugin suite is the recommended install. If you need specific skills only:

```
# Design only (generate and edit screens)
npx skills add google-labs-code/stitch-skills \
  --skills stitch::generate-design,stitch::manage-design-system,enhance-prompt

# Import existing code (full migration pipeline)
npx skills add google-labs-code/stitch-skills \
  --skills stitch::code-to-design,stitch::extract-design-md,stitch::extract-static-html,stitch::upload-to-stitch

# Code generation (Stitch to React)
npx skills add google-labs-code/stitch-skills \
  --skills react:components,shadcn-ui
```

> Many skills have inter-dependencies. Check the dependency listings above before installing selectively.
